common_name: Vernonburg Daylily (Buff Melon Self, Parent of Vick Mulkey)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in full sun and well-drained soil; this dormant diploid, registered by Joiner in 1966, opens buff melon self flowers in midseason.

directions: Registered by Joiner in 1966 from a cross of an unnamed seedling and Frances Fay, Vernonburg is a dormant diploid daylily bearing a buff melon self flower, about seven inches across on 24-inch scapes with extended bloom habit that open in midseason. It earned no AHS awards of its own. Joiner later used it as a parent of Vick Mulkey, an ancestor of the Lenington All-American Award winner Orange Velvet. Plant divisions in full sun in well-drained soil, dividing congested clumps every three to four years in spring to sustain vigorous flowering.

common_name: Louise Mercer Daylily (Rose Double with Green-Yellow Throat, Parent of Both Sides Now)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in full sun and well-drained, fertile soil; this dormant diploid double, registered by Joiner in 1973, opens rose self flowers with a green-yellow throat in midseason.

directions: Registered by Joiner in 1973, Louise Mercer is a dormant diploid double daylily bearing a rose self flower with a green-yellow throat, about five inches across on 18-inch scapes with extended bloom habit that open in midseason. It earned an AHS Honorable Mention in 1979. D. Kirchhoff later used it alongside Siloam Double Rose as a parent in the complex cross that produced Both Sides Now, an ancestor of the Ida Munson Award winner Mayor of Cornatzer. Plant divisions in full sun in well-drained, fertile soil, dividing congested clumps every three to four years in spring to maintain its double form.

common_name: Double Love Daylily (Pink and Peach Bitone Double, Parent of Both Sides Now)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in full sun and well-drained, fertile soil; this evergreen double, registered by B. Brown in 1972, opens pink and peach bitone flowers with a light gold throat early in midseason.

directions: Registered by B. Brown in 1972 from a cross of (President Giles x Double Decker) and an unnamed seedling, Double Love is an evergreen double daylily bearing a pink and peach bitone flower with a light gold throat, about five inches across on 26-inch scapes with extended bloom habit that open early in the midseason. It carries no AHS awards of its own. D. Kirchhoff later used it alongside Nagasaki as a parent in the complex cross that produced Both Sides Now, an ancestor of the Ida Munson Award winner Mayor of Cornatzer. Plant divisions in full sun in well-drained, fertile soil, dividing congested clumps every three to four years in spring to maintain its double form.

common_name: Jock Randall Daylily (Rose Self with Green-Yellow Throat, Parent of Illini Show Girl)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in full sun and well-drained soil; this evergreen tetraploid, registered by Peck in 1970, opens rose self flowers with a green-yellow throat in midseason.

directions: Registered by Peck in 1970 from a cross of an unnamed seedling and tetraploid Sanders Walker, Jock Randall is an evergreen tetraploid daylily bearing a rose self flower with a green-yellow throat, about six inches across on 29-inch scapes that open in midseason. It earned the AHS Award of Merit in 1976 after an Honorable Mention in 1973. Varner later crossed it with Ed Murray to produce Illini Show Girl, a parent of Ruby Sentinel and an ancestor of the President's Cup winner Mary Alice. Plant divisions in full sun in well-drained soil, dividing congested clumps every three to four years in spring to sustain vigorous flowering.

common_name: Lusty Lealand Daylily (Red Self with Green-Yellow Throat, Parent of Ed Marshall)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in full sun and well-drained soil; this evergreen tetraploid, registered by Peck in 1970, opens red self flowers with a green-yellow throat in midseason.

directions: Registered by Peck in 1970, Lusty Lealand is an evergreen tetraploid daylily bearing a red self flower with a green-yellow throat, about six inches across on 28-inch scapes that open in midseason. It earned an AHS Honorable Mention in 1973. Harris-Benz later used it in the complex cross with Mavis Smith that produced Ed Marshall, a parent of Ruby Sentinel and an ancestor of the President's Cup winner Mary Alice. Plant divisions in full sun in well-drained soil, dividing congested clumps every three to four years in spring to sustain vigorous flowering.

common_name: Mavis Smith Daylily (Pale Cream Flushed Pink, Parent of Ed Marshall)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in full sun and well-drained soil; this semi-evergreen diploid, registered by G. Lenington in 1974, opens pale cream flowers flushed pink in midseason.

directions: Registered by G. Lenington in 1974 from a cross of Mary Mae Simon and an unnamed seedling, Mavis Smith is a semi-evergreen diploid daylily bearing a pale cream flower flushed pink with a green throat, about five inches across on 33-inch scapes with extended bloom habit that open in midseason. It earned the AHS Award of Merit in 1981 after a Junior Citation in 1974 and an Honorable Mention in 1977. Harris-Benz later used it in the complex cross with Lusty Lealand that produced Ed Marshall, a parent of Ruby Sentinel and an ancestor of the President's Cup winner Mary Alice. Plant divisions in full sun in well-drained soil, dividing congested clumps every three to four years in spring to sustain vigorous flowering.

common_name: Grand Canyon Daylily (Fragrant Buff-Lavender Bicolor, Parent of Tim Tanner)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in full sun and well-drained, fertile soil; this evergreen diploid, registered by Farris in 1957, opens very fragrant buff and lavender bicolor flowers very early in the season.

directions: Registered by Farris in 1957, Grand Canyon is a very fragrant, reblooming evergreen diploid daylily bearing a buff and lavender bicolor flower on 24-inch scapes that open very early in the season. It earned the AHS Award of Merit in 1964 after an Honorable Mention in 1961. L. Simon later crossed it with Southern Heritage to produce Tim Tanner, a parent of Colonel Simon and, through that line, an ancestor of Orange Velvet. Plant divisions in full sun in well-drained, fertile soil, dividing congested clumps every three to four years in spring to maintain vigor.

common_name: Southern Heritage Daylily (Cream and Lilac Blend, Parent of Tim Tanner)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in full sun and well-drained, fertile soil; this evergreen diploid, registered by R.W. Munson in 1958, opens cream and lilac blend flowers on tall scapes in the midseason-to-late period.

directions: Registered by R.W. Munson in 1958 from a cross of Spring Waltz and an unnamed seedling, Southern Heritage is an evergreen diploid daylily bearing a cream and lilac blend flower on tall 42-inch scapes that open in the midseason-to-late period. It earned an AHS Junior Citation in 1959 and an Honorable Mention in 1962. L. Simon later crossed it with Grand Canyon to produce Tim Tanner, a parent of Colonel Simon and, through that line, an ancestor of Orange Velvet. Plant divisions in full sun in well-drained, fertile soil, dividing congested clumps every three to four years in spring to maintain vigor.

common_name: Solo Daylily (Fragrant Light Yellow Self, Parent of Jakarta)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in full sun and well-drained soil; this dormant diploid, registered by Branch in 1960, opens fragrant light yellow self flowers in midseason.

directions: Registered by Branch in 1960 from a cross of Strutter and an unnamed seedling, Solo is a fragrant dormant diploid daylily bearing a light yellow self flower with a green throat, about five and a half inches across on 32-inch scapes that open in midseason. It earned the AHS Award of Merit in 1966 after an Honorable Mention in 1962. Whatley later used it as a parent of Jakarta, which went on to parent Emerald Crown, an ancestor of the Lenington All-American Award winner Orange Velvet. Plant divisions in full sun in well-drained soil, dividing congested clumps every three to four years in spring to sustain vigorous flowering.
